title: Many Protestants admit a good-sense mortal/venial distinction for grave vs lighter regenerate sins
source_text: LXII. Praeterea patet ex dictis plurimos ex Protestantibus, nempe Theologos omnes Confessionis Augustanae, & nonnullos ex ipsis Reformatis, distinctionem peccati in mortale & veniale bono sensu sumptam admittere, & peccata mortalia singulari qua-dam ratione vocare peccata graviora atque atrociora, quae conscientiam vastant, & novo mortis aeternae reatu actu involvunt ipsos renatos & justificatos, quum in ea in-currunt: venialia vero peccata illa leviora, quae cum bona conscientia & sensu remis-sionis peccatorum consistere possunt, & per quae persona fidelis novo mortis aeternae reatu non obstringitur, nec inepta sit quae in regnum coelorum admittatur, etsi in aliquo tali peccato moriatur.
pass_a_gloss: Besides it is plain from what has been said that very many among Protestants—namely all the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, and some even among the Reformed—admit the distinction of sin into mortal and venial taken in a good sense, and call mortal sins in a certain singular way the heavier and more atrocious sins which waste the conscience and actually involve the regenerate and justified themselves in a new guilt of eternal death when they run into them: but venial those lighter sins which can stand with a good conscience and a sense of the remission of sins, and through which the faithful person is not bound with a new guilt of eternal death, nor is unfit to be admitted into the kingdom of heaven, even if he die in some such sin.
pass_b_english: Augustana across the board, and some Reformed, keep a good-sense mortal/venial vocabulary.
Mortal = conscience-wasting new death-guilt; venial = lighter faults compatible with peace, pardon-sense, and heaven-fitness even at death.

choices.why: Appropriated labels, not Rome’s intrinsic veniality.
